title: Enums and Pattern Matching
objectives: Construct unit and data-carrying variants; write enum methods and track ownership of payloads.
Handle absence with `Option`, optional references, safe lookup and checked arithmetic.
Match variants and bind payloads while respecting borrowed and owned inputs.
Make matches exhaustive with explicit alternatives, inclusive ranges and appropriate catch-alls.
Use `if let` for selected cases and `let...else` to leave early when required data is absent.

lessons.title: Defining enums
lessons.objective_md: Construct unit, tuple-payload and named-payload enum variants; write shared methods and predict owned-payload moves versus explicit Copy behavior.

screens.heading: An enum lists every possible kind

steps.caption_md: An **enum** (short for enumeration) is a type that lists every possible kind of value. Each kind is called a **variant**. A `Direction` is always exactly one of these four.
steps.visual_md: Type Direction: North / East / South / West; no local values yet.

steps.caption_md: `Direction::North` creates a value. The variant name is written after the enum name and `::`, because variants live **inside** the enum's namespace.
steps.visual_md: heading = Direction::North; one selected variant.

steps.caption_md: `next` holds a different variant of the same type. Both variables have type `Direction`, so a function that takes a `Direction` accepts either one.
steps.visual_md: heading = North; next = East; both values have type Direction.

steps.caption_md: `#[derive(Debug)]` lets you print a variant with `{:?}`. It prints the variant's name.
steps.visual_md: heading = North; next = East; stdout: North then East.

screens.heading: Variants live inside the enum's name
screens.text_md:
Variant names are **namespaced** under their enum. That's why you write `Direction::North`, not `North`.

This lets two enums both have a variant called `Up` (say, `Direction::Up` and `Volume::Up`) without clashing.

screens.heading: A struct is "and", an enum is "or"
screens.text_md:
A struct value has **all** of its fields at once: an `x` **and** a `y`.

An enum value is **one** of its variants: a `Quit` **or** a `Move` **or** a `Write`. Which one it is can change from value to value, but the list of possibilities is fixed.

Use a struct when every value has the same parts. Use an enum when a value is one of a few different kinds.

coming_from.c: Think of named cases in a tagged union or std::variant. Ordinary safe Rust patterns select the active variant and expose only its payload; these diagrams do not specify physical tag layout.
coming_from.go: Go-style const names illustrate unit cases, while distinct struct values illustrate payload shapes. A Rust enum gathers the declared alternatives into one type.
coming_from.java: A sealed hierarchy is a useful analogy for different cases carrying different data. Rust writes these alternatives in one enum declaration without inheritance.
coming_from.js: A TypeScript discriminated union is a useful comparison: a tag identifies which fields belong to the selected case. Rust declares those alternatives together in one enum.
coming_from.python: Python Enum provides named members; Rust variants additionally declare their own statically checked payload shapes. Constructing one Rust value selects one variant.

A value stores one selected variant and its associated data; diagrams do not promise discriminant sizes, field order, stack placement or exact addresses.

lessons.title: `Option`: a value that might be missing
lessons.objective_md: Represent absence with Option, distinguish None from present zero or empty text, and use safe lookup/conversion/checked arithmetic with explicit failure behavior.

screens.heading: Something, or nothing
screens.text_md:
Rust has **no null**. When a value might be missing, its type is **`Option<T>`**, an enum from the standard library with two variants: `Some(value)` or `None`.

`T` is the type inside: `Some(5)` is an `Option<i32>`, `Some('e')` an `Option<char>`.

`None` needs a type annotation here, because the compiler can't guess what kind of value is missing.

coming_from.c: C++ std::optional is a useful comparison. Rust code must explicitly choose how to handle Option; unwrap_or supplies a fallback. Option itself does not promise that every possible extraction API is non-panicking.
coming_from.go: A Go-style value/ok result separates data from presence. Rust groups that distinction into Some(value) or None, so a real zero is not mistaken for failure.
coming_from.java: Java Optional and nullable C# values are useful comparisons for explicit missing data. Rust Option works with numbers, references and owned text; it does not imply every value is a nullable pointer.
coming_from.js: With TypeScript strict-null checking, number or undefined can express missing data. Rust Option expresses the same kind of distinction as an enum, with Some and None cases.
coming_from.python: Python None illustrates absence. Option makes that possibility explicit in the Rust type: a plain i32 cannot silently become None. Some(0) is still a present number.

screens.heading: An `Option` is not the value inside
screens.text_md:
This error is the whole point of `Option`. To use the number, you must first say what happens when there **isn't** one.

In other languages, forgetting that check is a crash at run time. In Rust, it's a compile error.

screens.heading: Standard methods that might find nothing

steps.caption_md: `get(i)` is the safe way to index. Inside the range you get `Some`; past the end you get `None` instead of a crash.
steps.visual_md: scores = [10,20,30]; get(1) = Some(&20); get(5) = None.

steps.caption_md: `first()` and `last()` return `None` for an empty slice, so they return an `Option` too.
steps.visual_md: scores.first() = Some(&10); no array element is removed.

steps.caption_md: `find` gives the byte position of the first match, or `None` if there is no match. `s.chars().next()` works the same way: `None` for empty text.
steps.visual_md: "hello".find("l") = Some(2); "hello".find("z") = None; positions count bytes.

steps.caption_md: `to_digit(10)` converts an accepted ASCII radix digit to its value and returns `None` for other scalars. `char::from_digit(7, 10)` goes the other way and gives `Some('7')`.
steps.visual_md: '7'.to_digit(10) = Some(7); 'x'.to_digit(10) = None.

screens.heading: Arithmetic that can't overflow
screens.text_md:
`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul` and `checked_div` return an `Option`. You get `Some(result)` when the answer fits in the type, and `None` when it would overflow or divide by zero.

A plain `250u8 + 10` panics in a debug build. The checked version hands the problem back to you instead.

Correct. Not every character is a digit, so `to_digit` returns `Option<u32>`.
Correct. The result might not fit in a `u8`, so `checked_mul` returns `Option<u8>`. Here it's `None`, because 400 > 255.
Not quite. `contains` always has an answer, yes or no, so it returns a `bool`.

lessons.title: `match`
lessons.objective_md: Select and return a match arm, bind variant payloads and explain how shared versus owned matching affects the source owner.

screens.heading: A value flows to the arm it fits

steps.caption_md: `value_in_cents` receives `Coin::Dime`. The `match` will compare it with each **arm** in turn.
steps.visual_md: Input coin = Coin::Dime; candidate patterns: Penny / Nickel / Dime / Quarter.

steps.caption_md: The first arm's **pattern** is `Coin::Penny`. A dime doesn't fit, so Rust moves on.
steps.visual_md: Coin::Dime does not match Coin::Penny; no arm body runs.

steps.caption_md: `Coin::Nickel` doesn't fit either.
steps.visual_md: Coin::Dime does not match Coin::Nickel; no arm body runs.

steps.caption_md: `Coin::Dime` fits. Rust runs this arm's code, and its value, `10`, becomes the value of the whole `match`. The arms below are skipped.
steps.visual_md: Coin::Dime matches Coin::Dime; selected arm result = 10; Quarter arm is skipped.

steps.caption_md: The `match` was the function's last expression, so `10` is returned and printed.
steps.visual_md: value_in_cents returns 10; stdout: 10.

screens.heading: Each arm is `pattern => expression`
screens.text_md:
Each arm has a pattern, `=>`, and an expression. The arms are separated by commas.

For more than one line, use curly braces. The block's last expression is the arm's value, so `1` is still the result for a penny.

The whole `match` is an expression too, so you can return it or store it with `let`.

coming_from.c: A C `switch` compares integers and falls through unless you `break`. Rust's `match` never falls through, works on any enum, can bind the data inside a variant, and produces a value.
coming_from.go: Like Go's `switch`, it never falls through, and like a type switch it can bind the value inside. Unlike Go, Rust refuses to compile when a variant isn't handled.
coming_from.java: Close to Java's `switch` expressions with patterns (`case Circle c ->`) and C#'s `switch` expressions. Rust's `match` is always an expression, never falls through, and must cover every variant.
coming_from.js: Like `switch`, but with no fall-through and no `break`: exactly one arm runs. An arm can also pull data out of the value, and the whole `match` produces a value.
coming_from.python: Python 3.10's `match`/`case` is similar, and class patterns pull data out too. Rust's `match` also checks at compile time that every case is handled, and every arm must produce the same type.

screens.heading: Arms must produce compatible result types
screens.text_md: Because `match` produces a value, every arm must produce the **same type**. Rust needs to know the type of `value` before the program runs.

question.prompt_md: Which statement about the arms of a `match` is true?

options.text_md: Arms are checked from top to bottom, and only the first arm that fits runs.

Not quite. Exactly one arm runs: the first one whose pattern fits.

Not quite. That's C's `switch`. A Rust `match` never falls through to the next arm, so there's no `break`.

screens.heading: An Option payload can be a tuple
screens.text_md: A variant payload may itself be a tuple. Here Some((a,b)) combines the Some pattern with the tuple destructuring already learned in Chapter 3. The names are local to the matching arm. None has no pair to destructure. Later chapters generalize nesting to richer patterns.

fn main(){println!("{} {}",pair_sum(Some((2,3))),pair_sum(None));}

screens.heading: Forget a case, and it won't compile
screens.text_md:
A `match` must be **exhaustive**: every possible value needs an arm. Otherwise, what would `seconds` return for a yellow light?

This is a huge help when you add a variant to an enum later. Every `match` that forgot it becomes a compile error, with the line number.

screens.heading: Use `_` when you don't need the value

coming_from.c: `_` is `default:`. A compiler may warn about a missing enum case in a `switch` (`-Wswitch`); in Rust it's a hard error, E0004. Ranges like `1..=5` are built into patterns.
coming_from.go: `_` is like `default:`, and `1 | 2 =>` is like `case 1, 2:`. Go silently skips a `switch` when nothing matches; Rust won't compile until every value is covered.

screens.text_md:
`if let` is a `match` that cares about one pattern and ignores the rest. You write less, but you give up the exhaustiveness check: the compiler won't tell you about cases you forgot.

screens.heading: `match`, `if let` or `let...else`?
screens.text_md:
Use **`match`** when several cases each need different code.

Use **`if let`** when you only care about one pattern.
